newsitem.title: UK: Deutsche sees increased risk of EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche sees increased risk of EMU delay.

text.p: Germany's largest bank, Deutsche Bank, has advised clients there is a growing risk of problems in achieving European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) as scheduled.

At a time when market enthusiasm about the EMU process is running high, the bank's Deutsche Morgan Grenfell issued a note saying the probability of EMU being delayed, or not happening at all, had risen to 45 percent from 30 percent previously.

Bronwyn Curtis, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's head of economic and fixed income research, told Reuters on Tuesday that the bank had also organised a conference call with leading clients to advise them of the increased risks.
The research note said there was a 10 percent probability EMU would start with a larger group than the core European countries, compared with a 20 percent chance previously.

EMU is scheduled to start in 1999 but the decision on which member states qualify to take part at the start will be made early in 1998 based on governments' ability to meet the Maastricht criteria by the end of 1997.
Deutsche analysts said tensions between possible EMU members had recently increased in two critical areas.
The first was interpretation of Maastricht Treaty criteria.

"France, Italy and Spain are clearly opting for a more relaxed interpretation of the criteria, whereas Germany insists on a stricter interpretation, although it is prepared to allow some fudging," they said.
The second area of tension surrounded the details and strictness envisaged for the proposed "stability pact", a plan to enforce prudent fiscal policy after EMU starts.

"The delay in reaching a decision on the stability pact shows that some EU countries would also like to water down the stability pact," Deutsche analysts said. "A strict stability pact would, however, be the price to pay for Germany accepting some fudging of the criteria," the note said.
Meanwhile it said the German government is becoming increasingly concerned about the value of the new euro currency.

"While Chancellor Kohl clearly wants EMU to happen on time, he knows that to get the project up and running, euro credibility is essential," Deutsche analysts said. "Without this credibility he cannot sell the replacement for the mark to his electorate in an election year (1998)."
But, if EMU were postponed or abandoned, there would be short-term financial market implications to be considered which could damage Germany.

Deutsche analysts said these included a stronger mark and the spin-off effects of lower growth and pressure on the Bundesbank to cut interest rates further, which could in turn widen European bond spreads against Bunds.
